name: Gallstone Yellow
lede: Gallstone Yellow is a deep, brownish yellow named for the stones of the gall bladder, both as number 69 in a nineteenth-century color chart for naturalists and as an artists' pigment ground from the gallstones of oxen.

sections.title: Number 69 in Syme's chart
sections.body:
Gallstone Yellow is number 69 in the yellows of Patrick Syme's *Werner's Nomenclature of Colours*, a chart for naturalists [1][2]. Abraham Gottlob Werner had devised a list of 54 colors in 1774 to identify minerals [1]. Syme, an Edinburgh flower painter, expanded it to 108 colors in 1814 and 110 in 1821, and added a painted swatch for each [1][2].

Baty counts gallstone yellow among the terms that Syme introduced in 1814 [3]. In Baty's transcription the entry for number 69 does not carry the [W] mark that Syme used for Werner's own colors, though Baty also finds those marks inconsistent [4][5]. Whether Syme named the color for the stones themselves or for the pigment is not stated in Baty [3][4].

sections.title: Recipe, examples and swatch
sections.body:
Syme gave a recipe for each color. His number 69 starts from gamboge yellow, adds a small amount of Dutch orange and a minute touch of honey yellow [4]. The recipes also run the other way, since saffron yellow is made of gamboge yellow and gallstone yellow in about equal parts [4]. For examples from nature, Syme named gallstones for the animal and a marigold apple for the vegetable [6].

The swatch on this page, #A36629, is a brownish orange, darker and browner than a recipe of gamboge would suggest [6]. Our library calls it an aged swatch and approximate [6], and Baty warns that Syme's swatches have grown more muted with time, so surviving ones understate the original hues [7]. Its nearest names in our library are [[sudan-brown]] and [[ochre-brown]], and our name tables give the same screen color the name [[toffee]] [6]. Syme's own pale relatives are [[honey-yellow]] and [[saffron-yellow]], and the recipe starts from [[gamboge-yellow]] [4].

Do not confuse it with the ISCC-NBS color *gallstone*, which is a gold close to [[old-gold]] [8]. Maerz and Paul date that English color word to 1764 [8].

sections.title: The paint made from gallstones
sections.body:
Yellows from animal bile are much older than Syme's chart [9]. A Greek manuscript of the third century and an Italian one of the eighth describe fish gall ground with chalk and vinegar to give a color like [[orpiment]] [9]. Tortoise bile is mentioned for gilded letters [9]. A German manuscript of about 1470 and the Colmarer Kunstbuch, which calls the result *aureus lombarticus*, describe similar recipes, and Thompson uses the term Lombard gold for a bile yellow [9]. Gall of eels and gallstones are also reported in this context [9].

True gallstone pigment is a seventeenth-century matter. The English sources Hilliard and Norgate, and the French source Boutet in 1674, describe gallstones from oxen, which when ground gave a dark yellow [9]. St Clair adds that the stones were crushed and ground in gum water [10]. He lists it among the artists' yellows that were unpleasant to make, beside [[orpiment]] and gamboge, both highly poisonous [10].

The commercial story is thinner than the name suggests. In 1764 Dossie recommended ox bile as a substitute, and colourmen at the end of the eighteenth century took that up as *gallstone*, although it was rarely used [9]. By the nineteenth century commercial products were probably largely substitutes made from quercitron lakes, according to Harley [9]. Salter in 1869 praised gallstone as a deep-toned yellow giving richer tints than most yellows, and noted that the pigment sold under the name was often replaced by a more stable substitute [9]. By the early twentieth century Heaton listed it as obsolete or little used [9]. Payne, on the other hand, thought siennas inferior to gallstone [9].

sections.title: A color for the clinic
sections.body:
Syme's preface recommended the book for morbid anatomy, since conditions from inflammation to gangrene are strikingly marked by color [11]. Medicine took up the colors only slowly. In 1817 John Gordon used it to argue that the brain's grey substance is really Wood Brown, and in 1819 William Prout described urinary stones in Syme's terms, with an outer layer of wax yellow and an inner one of wood brown [12]. A medical illustration of gallbladder and gallstones serves in Baty's plates as the animal example for gallstone yellow [13].

Yellow has long been the color of sickness. St Clair points to sallow skin, jaundice and the bilious attack [10].

sections.title: In the naturalists' hands
sections.body: Naturalists used the numbers as shorthand. William Chapman Hewitson's *British Oology* of 1833 describes birds' eggs by Syme's colors, and matches the nightingale's to number 69, Gallstone Yellow [14]. In 1905 the authors of the French *Repertoire de couleurs* reused gallstone yellow, together with violet purple, primrose yellow and China blue, without realizing that the terms came from Syme [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of this swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 1,091 works, or 4.6 per cent [15]. The match rate is highest in the 1300s, at 12.4 per cent (31 of 251 paintings), and falls to 3.4 per cent in the 1700s (117 of 3,449) [15]. The peak decade is the 1430s, when 11 of 51 paintings match, 4.7 times the archive-wide rate [15]. The earliest match is a funerary papyrus of about 1069 BC, where it covers 29 per cent of the image [15].

Among painters, George Dawe has 18 matching paintings out of 50, [[painter:fra-angelico|Fra Angelico]] 5 out of 16 and [[painter:filippo-lippi|Filippo Lippi]] 4 out of 13 [15]. The widest matches are Toulouse-Lautrec's [[painting:met-437834|Mademoiselle Nys]], of 1899, at 58 per cent of the image, and a Chinese album of calligraphy and paintings by Bian Shoumin, of 1700, at 51 per cent [15]. [[painter:henri-de-toulouse-lautrec|Toulouse-Lautrec]]'s *La danse mauresque* of 1895 follows at 50 per cent [15].

The surprise is the role it plays. In the paintings that contain it, the color falls among the highlights in 56 cases out of 100, in the mid-tones in 41, and in the shadows in only 3 [15]. This brownish yellow behaves as a light in paint, not a dark. Gilded grounds and warm skin photographed under museum light may land here, and a color match cannot tell leaf from paint. As always these are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is a screen color, not a pigment test [15].

choices: Dutch orange and a minute proportion of honey yellow
questions.answer: Dutch orange and a minute proportion of honey yellow

openers: Syme's animal example for Gallstone Yellow is literally gallstones; the artists' pigment of the same name was ground from the stones of oxen.
The pigment's name outlived its material: by the 1800s what colourmen sold as gallstone was mostly a plant-dye substitute.
In paintings the Gallstone Yellow swatch works as a light: in 56 cases out of 100 it sits among the highlights.
